     6	
     7	# Frontend Design
     8	
     9	Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.
    10	
    11	## Ground your designs in the subject matter
    12	
    13	If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.
    14	
    15	## Design principles
    16	
    17	For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.
    18	
    19	Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.
    20	
    21	Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.
    22	
    23	Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.
    24	
    25	Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
    26	- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
    27	- Using all caps for labels.
    28	- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.
    29	
    30	Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.
    31	
    32	Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.
    33	
    34	Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.
    35	
    36	## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique
    37	
    38	For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
    39	1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
    40	2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
    41	3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
    42	4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
    43	5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.
    44	
    45	All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.
    46	
    47	Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
    48	- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
    49	- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
    50	- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
    51	- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.
    52	
    53	Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.
    54	
    55	When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.
    56	
    57	## Restraint and self-critique
    58	
    59	Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.
    60	
    61	## More on writing in design
    62	
    63	Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.
    64	
    65	Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.
    66	
    67	Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.
    68	
    69	Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.
    70	
    71	Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

"""
Joint Fe / Cu / citrate / chloride speciation solver.
25 C, I = 0.1 M. Constants from NIST 46, Baes & Mesmer (1976),
Martell & Smith Vol 3, Koenigsberger et al., and Bjerrum.
See CONSTANTS_TABLE below for exact values and provenance.
"""

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Thermodynamic database (25 C, I = 0.1 M unless noted)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

RT_F = 0.05916  # V / decade at 25 C, base-10
KW   = 1.0e-14  # ion product of water

# Citrate (H3L). pKa's are for I = 0.1 M (Martell & Smith Vol 3).
pKa = {"H3L": 3.13, "H2L": 4.76, "HL": 6.40}
Ka  = {k: 10 ** -v for k, v in pKa.items()}

# Fe(III) hydrolysis: Fe3+ + n H2O = Fe(OH)n^(3-n) + n H+ ; log*beta_n
# Baes & Mesmer 1976, extrapolated to I=0.1 M.
logbstar_FeIII_OH = {1: -2.19, 2: -5.67, 3: -13.6, 4: -21.6}
# Dimer 2Fe3+ + 2H2O = Fe2(OH)2^4+ + 2H+; kept out (minor at 1 mM & I=0.1M).

# Fe(III) chloride: Fe3+ + n Cl- = FeCl_n^(3-n) ; log beta_n
# NIST 46 (Byrne, Byrne-Kester extrapolation).
logb_FeIII_Cl = {1: 1.48, 2: 2.13, 3: 1.13}

# Fe(III) citrate. Koenigsberger et al. (2000) J.Inorg.Biochem 78:175;
# Silva et al. (2009) Dalton Trans. Choosing the mono- and dinuclear set.
logK_FeIII_L      = 11.40  # Fe3+ + L3-  = FeL(aq)
logK_FeIII_HL     = 12.30  # Fe3+ + HL2- = FeHL+
logb_FeIII_L2     = 15.60  # Fe3+ + 2L3- = FeL2^3-
logK_FeIII_L_OH   = 4.50   # FeL + OH-   = FeL(OH)-   (mixed hydroxo)

# Fe(OH)3(s) 2-line ferrihydrite: Fe(OH)3(s) + 3H+ = Fe3+ + 3H2O; log*Ks
logKs_FeOH3 = 3.5

# Fe(II) hydrolysis. Baes & Mesmer.
logbstar_FeII_OH = {1: -9.5}
# Fe(II) citrate. Martell & Smith.
logK_FeII_L  = 4.4  # Fe2+ + L3-  = FeL-
logK_FeII_HL = 3.2  # Fe2+ + HL2- = FeHL(aq)
# Fe(II) chloride (very weak).
logK_FeII_Cl = 0.14

# Cu(II) hydrolysis. Baes & Mesmer.
logbstar_CuII_OH = {1: -8.0, 2: -16.2, 3: -26.9, 4: -39.6}
# Cu(II) chloride. Bjerrum / NIST 46.
logb_CuII_Cl = {1: 0.40, 2: 0.16, 3: -2.29, 4: -4.59}
# Cu(II) citrate. NIST 46; polynuclear neglected above pH ~4 for 1 mM.
logK_CuII_L   = 5.90   # Cu2+ + L3-  = CuL-
logK_CuII_HL  = 3.42   # Cu2+ + HL2- = CuHL
logb_CuII_L2  = 8.50   # Cu2+ + 2L3- = CuL2^4-

# Cu(OH)2(s) (amorphous / freshly formed): Cu(OH)2(s) + 2H+ = Cu2+ + 2H2O
logKs_CuOH2 = 8.7   # ~1.0 log unit higher than tenorite CuO (7.65)

# Cu(I) chloride. Sugasaka & Fujii; NIST 46.
logb_CuI_Cl = {1: 3.0, 2: 5.5, 3: 5.7}
# CuCl(s) nantokite: CuCl(s) = Cu+ + Cl- ; log Ksp
logKsp_CuCl = -6.7

# Standard reduction potentials vs SHE (V).
E0 = {
    "Fe3+/Fe2+"    : 0.771,
    "Cu2+/Cu+"     : 0.153,
    "Cu2+/Cu(s)"   : 0.340,
    "Cu+/Cu(s)"    : 0.521,
    "Fe2+/Fe(s)"   : -0.44,
    "H+/H2"        : 0.000,
    "O2/H2O"       : 1.229,
}

# System composition
FE_T  = 1.0e-3    # 1 mM Fe total
CU_T  = 1.0e-3    # 1 mM Cu total
CL_T  = 0.1       # 0.1 M chloride (assumed ~constant)
CIT_T = 5.0e-3    # 5 mM citrate total


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper: side-reaction coefficients (alpha)
# alpha_M is [M_total_this_ox_state] / [M_free_ion]
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def alpha_FeIII(H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2):
    a = 1.0
    for n, lb in logbstar_FeIII_OH.items():
        a += 10**lb / H**n                      # hydrolysis
    for n, lb in logb_FeIII_Cl.items():
        a += 10**lb * Cl**n                     # chloride
    a += 10**logK_FeIII_L  * L3                 # FeL
    a += 10**logK_FeIII_HL * HL2                # FeHL+
    a += 10**logb_FeIII_L2 * L3**2              # FeL2^3-
    a += 10**logK_FeIII_L  * L3 * 10**logK_FeIII_L_OH * OH  # FeL(OH)-
    return a

def alpha_FeII(H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2):
    a = 1.0
    for n, lb in logbstar_FeII_OH.items():
        a += 10**lb / H**n
    a += 10**logK_FeII_L  * L3
    a += 10**logK_FeII_HL * HL2
    a += 10**logK_FeII_Cl * Cl
    return a

def alpha_CuII(H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2):
    a = 1.0
    for n, lb in logbstar_CuII_OH.items():
        a += 10**lb / H**n
    for n, lb in logb_CuII_Cl.items():
        a += 10**lb * Cl**n
    a += 10**logK_CuII_L  * L3
    a += 10**logK_CuII_HL * HL2
    a += 10**logb_CuII_L2 * L3**2
    return a

def alpha_CuI(Cl):
    a = 1.0
    for n, lb in logb_CuI_Cl.items():
        a += 10**lb * Cl**n
    return a


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Citrate acid-base speciation given free L3-
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def citrate_forms(H, L3):
    HL2  = L3  * H / Ka["HL"]
    H2L  = HL2 * H / Ka["H2L"]
    H3L  = H2L * H / Ka["H3L"]
    return H3L, H2L, HL2, L3


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Full speciation at one (pH, E)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def solve_point(pH, E, Cl=CL_T,
                Fe_T=FE_T, Cu_T=CU_T, Cit_T=CIT_T):
    """
    Returns a dict with all species concentrations plus flags for any
    saturated solid phases. Enforces mass balance on citrate; caps free
    Fe3+, Cu2+, Cu+ if a solid saturates.
    """
    H  = 10 ** -pH
    OH = KW / H

    # redox ratios of *free ions*
    r_Fe = 10 ** ((E - E0["Fe3+/Fe2+"]) / RT_F)   # [Fe3+]/[Fe2+]
    r_Cu = 10 ** ((E - E0["Cu2+/Cu+"])  / RT_F)   # [Cu2+]/[Cu+]

    # solubility caps (free ion at saturation of a candidate solid)
    Fe3_cap   = 10 **  logKs_FeOH3 * H**3     # cap from Fe(OH)3(s)
    Cu2_cap   = 10 **  logKs_CuOH2 * H**2     # cap from Cu(OH)2(s)
    Cu1_capCl = 10 **  logKsp_CuCl / Cl       # cap from CuCl(s)
    Cu1_capMe = 10 ** ((E - E0["Cu+/Cu(s)"]) / RT_F)  # cap from Cu(s)

    def cit_residual(logL):
        L3  = 10 ** logL
        H3L, H2L, HL2, _ = citrate_forms(H, L3)

        # side-reaction coefficients depend on L3, HL2
        aFe3 = alpha_FeIII(H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
        aFe2 = alpha_FeII (H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
        aCu2 = alpha_CuII (H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
        aCu1 = alpha_CuI  (Cl)

        # Free ions from mass balance for each redox state
        # Fe_T = [Fe3+] aFe3 + [Fe2+] aFe2, with [Fe2+] = [Fe3+]/r_Fe
        Fe3 = Fe_T / (aFe3 + aFe2 / r_Fe)
        # solid cap
        Fe3 = min(Fe3, Fe3_cap)
        Fe2 = Fe3 / r_Fe

        # Cu
        Cu2 = Cu_T / (aCu2 + aCu1 / r_Cu)
        Cu2 = min(Cu2, Cu2_cap)
        Cu1 = Cu2 / r_Cu
        # cap on Cu+ (whichever solid activates first)
        Cu1_cap = min(Cu1_capCl, Cu1_capMe)
        if Cu1 > Cu1_cap:
            Cu1 = Cu1_cap
            Cu2 = Cu1 * r_Cu  # follows redox equilibrium in solution

        # bound citrate (mol/L, with stoichiometric weight)
        bound  = Fe3 * (10**logK_FeIII_L * L3
                        + 10**logK_FeIII_HL * HL2
                        + 2 * 10**logb_FeIII_L2 * L3**2
                        + 10**logK_FeIII_L * L3 * 10**logK_FeIII_L_OH * OH)
        bound += Fe2 * (10**logK_FeII_L * L3 + 10**logK_FeII_HL * HL2)
        bound += Cu2 * (10**logK_CuII_L * L3
                        + 10**logK_CuII_HL * HL2
                        + 2 * 10**logb_CuII_L2 * L3**2)
        free_cit = H3L + H2L + HL2 + L3
        return free_cit + bound - Cit_T

    # bracket the log10 of free [L3-]
    try:
        logL_sol = brentq(cit_residual, -25.0, -0.5, xtol=1e-6, rtol=1e-8)
    except ValueError:
        # residual doesn't change sign in bracket; snap to bounds
        r_lo, r_hi = cit_residual(-25.0), cit_residual(-0.5)
        logL_sol = -25.0 if abs(r_lo) < abs(r_hi) else -0.5

    L3  = 10 ** logL_sol
    H3L, H2L, HL2, _ = citrate_forms(H, L3)

    aFe3 = alpha_FeIII(H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
    aFe2 = alpha_FeII (H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
    aCu2 = alpha_CuII (H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
    aCu1 = alpha_CuI  (Cl)

    Fe3 = Fe_T / (aFe3 + aFe2 / r_Fe)
    ferrihydrite = False
    if Fe3 > Fe3_cap:
        Fe3 = Fe3_cap
        ferrihydrite = True
    Fe2 = Fe3 / r_Fe

    Cu2 = Cu_T / (aCu2 + aCu1 / r_Cu)
    cu_oh2 = False
    if Cu2 > Cu2_cap:
        Cu2 = Cu2_cap
        cu_oh2 = True
    Cu1 = Cu2 / r_Cu
    cucl_s = False; cu_metal = False
    if Cu1 > Cu1_capCl and Cu1_capCl <= Cu1_capMe:
        Cu1 = Cu1_capCl; cucl_s = True
        Cu2 = Cu1 * r_Cu
    if Cu1 > Cu1_capMe:
        Cu1 = Cu1_capMe; cu_metal = True
        Cu2 = Cu1 * r_Cu

    # Enumerate species. Concentrations in mol/L.
    Fe3_species = {
        "Fe3+"        : Fe3,
        "FeOH2+"      : Fe3 * 10**logbstar_FeIII_OH[1] / H,
        "Fe(OH)2+"    : Fe3 * 10**logbstar_FeIII_OH[2] / H**2,
        "Fe(OH)3(aq)" : Fe3 * 10**logbstar_FeIII_OH[3] / H**3,
        "Fe(OH)4-"    : Fe3 * 10**logbstar_FeIII_OH[4] / H**4,
        "FeCl2+"      : Fe3 * 10**logb_FeIII_Cl[1] * Cl,
        "FeCl2+_"     : Fe3 * 10**logb_FeIII_Cl[2] * Cl**2,  # FeCl2+ (n=2)
        "FeCl3(aq)"   : Fe3 * 10**logb_FeIII_Cl[3] * Cl**3,
        "FeCit(aq)"   : Fe3 * 10**logK_FeIII_L * L3,
        "FeHCit+"     : Fe3 * 10**logK_FeIII_HL * HL2,
        "FeCit2^3-"   : Fe3 * 10**logb_FeIII_L2 * L3**2,
        "FeCit(OH)-"  : Fe3 * 10**logK_FeIII_L * L3 * 10**logK_FeIII_L_OH * OH,
    }
    Fe2_species = {
        "Fe2+"        : Fe2,
        "FeOH+"       : Fe2 * 10**logbstar_FeII_OH[1] / H,
        "FeCit-"      : Fe2 * 10**logK_FeII_L  * L3,
        "FeHCit(aq)"  : Fe2 * 10**logK_FeII_HL * HL2,
        "FeCl+"       : Fe2 * 10**logK_FeII_Cl * Cl,
    }
    Cu2_species = {
        "Cu2+"        : Cu2,
        "CuOH+"       : Cu2 * 10**logbstar_CuII_OH[1] / H,
        "Cu(OH)2(aq)" : Cu2 * 10**logbstar_CuII_OH[2] / H**2,
        "Cu(OH)3-"    : Cu2 * 10**logbstar_CuII_OH[3] / H**3,
        "Cu(OH)4^2-"  : Cu2 * 10**logbstar_CuII_OH[4] / H**4,
        "CuCl+"       : Cu2 * 10**logb_CuII_Cl[1] * Cl,
        "CuCl2(aq)"   : Cu2 * 10**logb_CuII_Cl[2] * Cl**2,
        "CuCl3-"      : Cu2 * 10**logb_CuII_Cl[3] * Cl**3,
        "CuCl4^2-"    : Cu2 * 10**logb_CuII_Cl[4] * Cl**4,
        "CuCit-"      : Cu2 * 10**logK_CuII_L  * L3,
        "CuHCit(aq)"  : Cu2 * 10**logK_CuII_HL * HL2,
        "CuCit2^4-"   : Cu2 * 10**logb_CuII_L2 * L3**2,
    }
    Cu1_species = {
        "Cu+"         : Cu1,
        "CuCl(aq)"    : Cu1 * 10**logb_CuI_Cl[1] * Cl,
        "CuCl2-"      : Cu1 * 10**logb_CuI_Cl[2] * Cl**2,
        "CuCl3^2-"    : Cu1 * 10**logb_CuI_Cl[3] * Cl**3,
    }
    cit_species = {
        "H3Cit"       : H3L,
        "H2Cit-"      : H2L,
        "HCit2-"      : HL2,
        "Cit3-"       : L3,
    }

    out = {
        "pH": pH, "E": E, "Cl": Cl,
        "H": H, "OH": OH,
        "Fe3_free": Fe3, "Fe2_free": Fe2,
        "Cu2_free": Cu2, "Cu1_free": Cu1,

{"language": "python", "code": """"
Joint Fe / Cu / citrate / chloride speciation solver.
25 C, I = 0.1 M. Constants from NIST 46, Baes & Mesmer (1976),
Martell & Smith Vol 3, Koenigsberger et al., and Bjerrum.
See CONSTANTS_TABLE below for exact values and provenance.
"""

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Thermodynamic database (25 C, I = 0.1 M unless noted)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

RT_F = 0.05916  # V / decade at 25 C, base-10
KW   = 1.0e-14  # ion product of water

# Citrate (H3L). pKa's are for I = 0.1 M (Martell & Smith Vol 3).
pKa = {"H3L": 3.13, "H2L": 4.76, "HL": 6.40}
Ka  = {k: 10 ** -v for k, v in pKa.items()}

# Fe(III) hydrolysis: Fe3+ + n H2O = Fe(OH)n^(3-n) + n H+ ; log*beta_n
# Baes & Mesmer 1976, extrapolated to I=0.1 M.
logbstar_FeIII_OH = {1: -2.19, 2: -5.67, 3: -13.6, 4: -21.6}
# Dimer 2Fe3+ + 2H2O = Fe2(OH)2^4+ + 2H+; kept out (minor at 1 mM & I=0.1M).

# Fe(III) chloride: Fe3+ + n Cl- = FeCl_n^(3-n) ; log beta_n
# NIST 46 (Byrne, Byrne-Kester extrapolation).
logb_FeIII_Cl = {1: 1.48, 2: 2.13, 3: 1.13}

# Fe(III) citrate. Koenigsberger et al. (2000) J.Inorg.Biochem 78:175;
# Silva et al. (2009) Dalton Trans. Choosing the mono- and dinuclear set.
logK_FeIII_L      = 11.40  # Fe3+ + L3-  = FeL(aq)
logK_FeIII_HL     = 12.30  # Fe3+ + HL2- = FeHL+
logb_FeIII_L2     = 15.60  # Fe3+ + 2L3- = FeL2^3-
logK_FeIII_L_OH   = 4.50   # FeL + OH-   = FeL(OH)-   (mixed hydroxo)

# Fe(OH)3(s) 2-line ferrihydrite: Fe(OH)3(s) + 3H+ = Fe3+ + 3H2O; log*Ks
logKs_FeOH3 = 3.5

# Fe(II) hydrolysis. Baes & Mesmer.
logbstar_FeII_OH = {1: -9.5}
# Fe(II) citrate. Martell & Smith.
logK_FeII_L  = 4.4  # Fe2+ + L3-  = FeL-
logK_FeII_HL = 3.2  # Fe2+ + HL2- = FeHL(aq)
# Fe(II) chloride (very weak).
logK_FeII_Cl = 0.14

# Cu(II) hydrolysis. Baes & Mesmer.
logbstar_CuII_OH = {1: -8.0, 2: -16.2, 3: -26.9, 4: -39.6}
# Cu(II) chloride. Bjerrum / NIST 46.
logb_CuII_Cl = {1: 0.40, 2: 0.16, 3: -2.29, 4: -4.59}
# Cu(II) citrate. NIST 46; polynuclear neglected above pH ~4 for 1 mM.
logK_CuII_L   = 5.90   # Cu2+ + L3-  = CuL-
logK_CuII_HL  = 3.42   # Cu2+ + HL2- = CuHL
logb_CuII_L2  = 8.50   # Cu2+ + 2L3- = CuL2^4-

# Cu(OH)2(s) (amorphous / freshly formed): Cu(OH)2(s) + 2H+ = Cu2+ + 2H2O
logKs_CuOH2 = 8.7   # ~1.0 log unit higher than tenorite CuO (7.65)

# Cu(I) chloride. Sugasaka & Fujii; NIST 46.
logb_CuI_Cl = {1: 3.0, 2: 5.5, 3: 5.7}
# CuCl(s) nantokite: CuCl(s) = Cu+ + Cl- ; log Ksp
logKsp_CuCl = -6.7

# Standard reduction potentials vs SHE (V).
E0 = {
    "Fe3+/Fe2+"    : 0.771,
    "Cu2+/Cu+"     : 0.153,
    "Cu2+/Cu(s)"   : 0.340,
    "Cu+/Cu(s)"    : 0.521,
    "Fe2+/Fe(s)"   : -0.44,
    "H+/H2"        : 0.000,
    "O2/H2O"       : 1.229,
}

# System composition
FE_T  = 1.0e-3    # 1 mM Fe total
CU_T  = 1.0e-3    # 1 mM Cu total
CL_T  = 0.1       # 0.1 M chloride (assumed ~constant)
CIT_T = 5.0e-3    # 5 mM citrate total


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper: side-reaction coefficients (alpha)
# alpha_M is [M_total_this_ox_state] / [M_free_ion]
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def alpha_FeIII(H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2):
    a = 1.0
    for n, lb in logbstar_FeIII_OH.items():
        a += 10**lb / H**n                      # hydrolysis
    for n, lb in logb_FeIII_Cl.items():
        a += 10**lb * Cl**n                     # chloride
    a += 10**logK_FeIII_L  * L3                 # FeL
    a += 10**logK_FeIII_HL * HL2                # FeHL+
    a += 10**logb_FeIII_L2 * L3**2              # FeL2^3-
    a += 10**logK_FeIII_L  * L3 * 10**logK_FeIII_L_OH * OH  # FeL(OH)-
    return a

def alpha_FeII(H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2):
    a = 1.0
    for n, lb in logbstar_FeII_OH.items():
        a += 10**lb / H**n
    a += 10**logK_FeII_L  * L3
    a += 10**logK_FeII_HL * HL2
    a += 10**logK_FeII_Cl * Cl
    return a

def alpha_CuII(H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2):
    a = 1.0
    for n, lb in logbstar_CuII_OH.items():
        a += 10**lb / H**n
    for n, lb in logb_CuII_Cl.items():
        a += 10**lb * Cl**n
    a += 10**logK_CuII_L  * L3
    a += 10**logK_CuII_HL * HL2
    a += 10**logb_CuII_L2 * L3**2
    return a

def alpha_CuI(Cl):
    a = 1.0
    for n, lb in logb_CuI_Cl.items():
        a += 10**lb * Cl**n
    return a


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Citrate acid-base speciation given free L3-
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def citrate_forms(H, L3):
    HL2  = L3  * H / Ka["HL"]
    H2L  = HL2 * H / Ka["H2L"]
    H3L  = H2L * H / Ka["H3L"]
    return H3L, H2L, HL2, L3


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Full speciation at one (pH, E)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def solve_point(pH, E, Cl=CL_T,
                Fe_T=FE_T, Cu_T=CU_T, Cit_T=CIT_T):
    """
    Returns a dict with all species concentrations plus flags for any
    saturated solid phases. Enforces mass balance on citrate; caps free
    Fe3+, Cu2+, Cu+ if a solid saturates.
    """
    H  = 10 ** -pH
    OH = KW / H

    # redox ratios of *free ions*
    r_Fe = 10 ** ((E - E0["Fe3+/Fe2+"]) / RT_F)   # [Fe3+]/[Fe2+]
    r_Cu = 10 ** ((E - E0["Cu2+/Cu+"])  / RT_F)   # [Cu2+]/[Cu+]

    # solubility caps (free ion at saturation of a candidate solid)
    Fe3_cap   = 10 **  logKs_FeOH3 * H**3     # cap from Fe(OH)3(s)
    Cu2_cap   = 10 **  logKs_CuOH2 * H**2     # cap from Cu(OH)2(s)
    Cu1_capCl = 10 **  logKsp_CuCl / Cl       # cap from CuCl(s)
    Cu1_capMe = 10 ** ((E - E0["Cu+/Cu(s)"]) / RT_F)  # cap from Cu(s)

    def cit_residual(logL):
        L3  = 10 ** logL
        H3L, H2L, HL2, _ = citrate_forms(H, L3)

        # side-reaction coefficients depend on L3, HL2
        aFe3 = alpha_FeIII(H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
        aFe2 = alpha_FeII (H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
        aCu2 = alpha_CuII (H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
        aCu1 = alpha_CuI  (Cl)

        # Free ions from mass balance for each redox state
        # Fe_T = [Fe3+] aFe3 + [Fe2+] aFe2, with [Fe2+] = [Fe3+]/r_Fe
        Fe3 = Fe_T / (aFe3 + aFe2 / r_Fe)
        # solid cap
        Fe3 = min(Fe3, Fe3_cap)
        Fe2 = Fe3 / r_Fe

        # Cu
        Cu2 = Cu_T / (aCu2 + aCu1 / r_Cu)
        Cu2 = min(Cu2, Cu2_cap)
        Cu1 = Cu2 / r_Cu
        # cap on Cu+ (whichever solid activates first)
        Cu1_cap = min(Cu1_capCl, Cu1_capMe)
        if Cu1 > Cu1_cap:
            Cu1 = Cu1_cap
            Cu2 = Cu1 * r_Cu  # follows redox equilibrium in solution

        # bound citrate (mol/L, with stoichiometric weight)
        bound  = Fe3 * (10**logK_FeIII_L * L3
                        + 10**logK_FeIII_HL * HL2
                        + 2 * 10**logb_FeIII_L2 * L3**2
                        + 10**logK_FeIII_L * L3 * 10**logK_FeIII_L_OH * OH)
        bound += Fe2 * (10**logK_FeII_L * L3 + 10**logK_FeII_HL * HL2)
        bound += Cu2 * (10**logK_CuII_L * L3
                        + 10**logK_CuII_HL * HL2
                        + 2 * 10**logb_CuII_L2 * L3**2)
        free_cit = H3L + H2L + HL2 + L3
        return free_cit + bound - Cit_T

    # bracket the log10 of free [L3-]
    try:
        logL_sol = brentq(cit_residual, -25.0, -0.5, xtol=1e-6, rtol=1e-8)
    except ValueError:
        # residual doesn't change sign in bracket; snap to bounds
        r_lo, r_hi = cit_residual(-25.0), cit_residual(-0.5)
        logL_sol = -25.0 if abs(r_lo) < abs(r_hi) else -0.5

    L3  = 10 ** logL_sol
    H3L, H2L, HL2, _ = citrate_forms(H, L3)

    aFe3 = alpha_FeIII(H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
    aFe2 = alpha_FeII (H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
    aCu2 = alpha_CuII (H, OH, Cl, L3, HL2)
    aCu1 = alpha_CuI  (Cl)

    Fe3 = Fe_T / (aFe3 + aFe2 / r_Fe)
    ferrihydrite = False
    if Fe3 > Fe3_cap:
        Fe3 = Fe3_cap
        ferrihydrite = True
    Fe2 = Fe3 / r_Fe

    Cu2 = Cu_T / (aCu2 + aCu1 / r_Cu)
    cu_oh2 = False
    if Cu2 > Cu2_cap:
        Cu2 = Cu2_cap
        cu_oh2 = True
    Cu1 = Cu2 / r_Cu
    cucl_s = False; cu_metal = False
    if Cu1 > Cu1_capCl and Cu1_capCl <= Cu1_capMe:
        Cu1 = Cu1_capCl; cucl_s = True
        Cu2 = Cu1 * r_Cu
    if Cu1 > Cu1_capMe:
        Cu1 = Cu1_capMe; cu_metal = True
        Cu2 = Cu1 * r_Cu

    # Enumerate species. Concentrations in mol/L.
    Fe3_species = {
        "Fe3+"        : Fe3,
        "FeOH2+"      : Fe3 * 10**logbstar_FeIII_OH[1] / H,
        "Fe(OH)2+"    : Fe3 * 10**logbstar_FeIII_OH[2] / H**2,
        "Fe(OH)3(aq)" : Fe3 * 10**logbstar_FeIII_OH[3] / H**3,
        "Fe(OH)4-"    : Fe3 * 10**logbstar_FeIII_OH[4] / H**4,
        "FeCl2+"      : Fe3 * 10**logb_FeIII_Cl[1] * Cl,
        "FeCl2+_"     : Fe3 * 10**logb_FeIII_Cl[2] * Cl**2,  # FeCl2+ (n=2)
        "FeCl3(aq)"   : Fe3 * 10**logb_FeIII_Cl[3] * Cl**3,
        "FeCit(aq)"   : Fe3 * 10**logK_FeIII_L * L3,
        "FeHCit+"     : Fe3 * 10**logK_FeIII_HL * HL2,
        "FeCit2^3-"   : Fe3 * 10**logb_FeIII_L2 * L3**2,
        "FeCit(OH)-"  : Fe3 * 10**logK_FeIII_L * L3 * 10**logK_FeIII_L_OH * OH,
    }
    Fe2_species = {
        "Fe2+"        : Fe2,
        "FeOH+"       : Fe2 * 10**logbstar_FeII_OH[1] / H,
        "FeCit-"      : Fe2 * 10**logK_FeII_L  * L3,
        "FeHCit(aq)"  : Fe2 * 10**logK_FeII_HL * HL2,
        "FeCl+"       : Fe2 * 10**logK_FeII_Cl * Cl,
    }
    Cu2_species = {
        "Cu2+"        : Cu2,
        "CuOH+"       : Cu2 * 10**logbstar_CuII_OH[1] / H,
        "Cu(OH)2(aq)" : Cu2 * 10**logbstar_CuII_OH[2] / H**2,
        "Cu(OH)3-"    : Cu2 * 10**logbstar_CuII_OH[3] / H**3,
        "Cu(OH)4^2-"  : Cu2 * 10**logbstar_CuII_OH[4] / H**4,
        "CuCl+"       : Cu2 * 10**logb_CuII_Cl[1] * Cl,
        "CuCl2(aq)"   : Cu2 * 10**logb_CuII_Cl[2] * Cl**2,
        "CuCl3-"      : Cu2 * 10**logb_CuII_Cl[3] * Cl**3,
        "CuCl4^2-"    : Cu2 * 10**logb_CuII_Cl[4] * Cl**4,
        "CuCit-"      : Cu2 * 10**logK_CuII_L  * L3,
        "CuHCit(aq)"  : Cu2 * 10**logK_CuII_HL * HL2,
        "CuCit2^4-"   : Cu2 * 10**logb_CuII_L2 * L3**2,
    }
    Cu1_species = {
        "Cu+"         : Cu1,
        "CuCl(aq)"    : Cu1 * 10**logb_CuI_Cl[1] * Cl,
        "CuCl2-"      : Cu1 * 10**logb_CuI_Cl[2] * Cl**2,
        "CuCl3^2-"    : Cu1 * 10**logb_CuI_Cl[3] * Cl**3,
    }
    cit_species = {
        "H3Cit"       : H3L,
        "H2Cit-"      : H2L,
        "HCit2-"      : HL2,
        "Cit3-"       : L3,
    }

    out = {
        "pH": pH, "E": E, "Cl": Cl,
        "H": H, "OH": OH,
        "Fe3_free": Fe3, "Fe2_free": Fe2,
        "Cu2_free": Cu2, "Cu1_free": Cu1,
        "L3_free": L3, "HL2": HL2, "H2L": H2L, "H3L": H3L,
        "Fe3_species": Fe3_species,
        "Fe2_species": Fe2_species,
        "Cu2_species": Cu2_species,
        "Cu1_species": Cu1_species,
        "cit_species": cit_species,
        "Fe3_sum": sum(Fe3_species.values()),
        "Fe2_sum": sum(Fe2_species.values()),
        "Cu2_sum": sum(Cu2_species.values()),
        "Cu1_sum": sum(Cu1_species.values()),
        "solids": {
            "Fe(OH)3(s)"  : ferrihydrite,
            "Cu(OH)2(s)"  : cu_oh2,
            "CuCl(s)"     : cucl_s,
            "Cu(s)"       : cu_metal,
        },
    }
    return out

"""
Compute the E-pH grid and species-vs-pH cuts, produce SVG figures.
"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap, BoundaryNorm
import json
import os

from speciation import (
    solve_point, E0, RT_F, KW,
    FE_T, CU_T, CIT_T, CL_T,
)

OUT = "/home/claude/figs"
os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. E-pH grid
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

pH_grid = np.arange(2.0, 10.001, 0.1)
E_grid  = np.arange(-0.40, 1.001, 0.02)

nP, nE = len(pH_grid), len(E_grid)
print(f"Grid: {nP} pH x {nE} E = {nP*nE} points")

# For each grid point, record which Fe / Cu species (or solid) dominates
# We group species into a small palette for readability.

FE_GROUPS = [
    ("Fe(s)",            {}),                    # placeholder, not used here
    ("Fe(OH)3(s)",       {"solid": "Fe(OH)3(s)"}),
    ("Fe3+ / hydroxo",   {"members": ["Fe3+", "FeOH2+", "Fe(OH)2+",
                                       "Fe(OH)3(aq)", "Fe(OH)4-"]}),
    ("Fe(III)-Cl",       {"members": ["FeCl2+", "FeCl2+_", "FeCl3(aq)"]}),
    ("Fe(III)-citrate",  {"members": ["FeCit(aq)", "FeHCit+",
                                       "FeCit2^3-", "FeCit(OH)-"]}),
    ("Fe2+ / hydroxo",   {"members": ["Fe2+", "FeOH+", "FeCl+"]}),
    ("Fe(II)-citrate",   {"members": ["FeCit-", "FeHCit(aq)"]}),
]

CU_GROUPS = [
    ("Cu(s)",            {"solid": "Cu(s)"}),
    ("CuCl(s)",          {"solid": "CuCl(s)"}),
    ("Cu(OH)2(s)",       {"solid": "Cu(OH)2(s)"}),
    ("Cu2+ / hydroxo",   {"members": ["Cu2+", "CuOH+", "Cu(OH)2(aq)",
                                       "Cu(OH)3-", "Cu(OH)4^2-"]}),
    ("Cu(II)-Cl",        {"members": ["CuCl+", "CuCl2(aq)",
                                       "CuCl3-", "CuCl4^2-"]}),
    ("Cu(II)-citrate",   {"members": ["CuCit-", "CuHCit(aq)", "CuCit2^4-"]}),
    ("Cu(I)-Cl",         {"members": ["Cu+", "CuCl(aq)", "CuCl2-",
                                       "CuCl3^2-"]}),
]

def group_fraction(species_dicts, group_defs, total, solids, redox_totals):
    """
    For an element, return a dict {group_name: fraction_of_total}.
    'redox_totals' is dict of ox-state totals to be summed.
    Solid groups get whatever is missing from the aqueous total.
    """
    fractions = {name: 0.0 for name, _ in group_defs}
    aqueous_sum = 0.0
    for sp_dict in species_dicts:
        for sp, c in sp_dict.items():
            aqueous_sum += c
            for name, spec in group_defs:
                members = spec.get("members", [])
                if sp in members:
                    fractions[name] += c
                    break

    # solids
    for name, spec in group_defs:
        solid = spec.get("solid")
        if solid and solids.get(solid, False):
            fractions[name] = max(fractions[name],
                                  max(0.0, total - aqueous_sum))

    # normalise; if solid present, may already exceed total slightly
    tot = sum(fractions.values())
    if tot <= 0:
        return fractions
    return {k: v / tot for k, v in fractions.items()}

fe_dom = np.full((nE, nP), -1, dtype=int)
cu_dom = np.full((nE, nP), -1, dtype=int)
# also record fractions for citrate partitioning at oxic E
cit_bound_fe = np.zeros(nP)
cit_bound_cu = np.zeros(nP)
cit_free     = np.zeros(nP)

# Also collect species fraction curves at specific E values
E_OXIC   = 0.60    # V vs SHE
E_MID    = 0.20
E_REDUCE = -0.20

cuts = {E_OXIC: [], E_MID: [], E_REDUCE: []}

for iE, E in enumerate(E_grid):
    for iP, pH in enumerate(pH_grid):
        r = solve_point(pH, E)

        # Fe grouping
        fe_frac = group_fraction(
            [r["Fe3_species"], r["Fe2_species"]],
            FE_GROUPS, FE_T, r["solids"],
            redox_totals={"Fe3": r["Fe3_sum"], "Fe2": r["Fe2_sum"]})
        # pick dominant
        dom_fe = max(fe_frac.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])
        fe_dom[iE, iP] = [n for n, _ in FE_GROUPS].index(dom_fe[0])

        # Cu grouping
        cu_frac = group_fraction(
            [r["Cu2_species"], r["Cu1_species"]],
            CU_GROUPS, CU_T, r["solids"],
            redox_totals={"Cu2": r["Cu2_sum"], "Cu1": r["Cu1_sum"]})
        dom_cu = max(cu_frac.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])
        cu_dom[iE, iP] = [n for n, _ in CU_GROUPS].index(dom_cu[0])

for E_pick in cuts:
    for pH in pH_grid:
        r = solve_point(pH, E_pick)
        cuts[E_pick].append(r)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Colour palette
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

FE_COLORS = {
    "Fe(s)"           : "#4a4a4a",
    "Fe(OH)3(s)"      : "#7a3b17",   # rust brown
    "Fe3+ / hydroxo"  : "#c98a4b",   # amber
    "Fe(III)-Cl"      : "#d3b26b",   # ochre
    "Fe(III)-citrate" : "#3f6d4e",   # dark olive/teal
    "Fe2+ / hydroxo"  : "#7fa15c",   # pale olive-green (Fe(II))
    "Fe(II)-citrate"  : "#274b3a",   # deep green
}
CU_COLORS = {
    "Cu(s)"           : "#8b5a3c",   # copper
    "CuCl(s)"         : "#c7c7ba",   # nantokite off-white
    "Cu(OH)2(s)"      : "#3a7d99",   # cyan-teal
    "Cu2+ / hydroxo"  : "#3f7bb6",   # azure Cu(II)
    "Cu(II)-Cl"       : "#6aa3c9",   # pale steel-blue
    "Cu(II)-citrate"  : "#2d4d7a",   # deep blue
    "Cu(I)-Cl"        : "#a89b6b",   # dull khaki (Cu(I))
}

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Plot Pourbaix-style maps
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

def plot_map(dom, groups, colors, title, fname):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 5.0), dpi=110)
    names  = [n for n, _ in groups]
    cmap   = ListedColormap([colors[n] for n in names])
    bounds = np.arange(-0.5, len(names) + 0.5, 1)
    norm   = BoundaryNorm(bounds, cmap.N)

    ax.pcolormesh(pH_grid, E_grid, dom, cmap=cmap, norm=norm, shading="auto")

    # water stability lines
    ax.plot(pH_grid, -RT_F * pH_grid, ls="--", lw=1.0, color="#333",
            alpha=0.7)
    ax.plot(pH_grid, 1.229 - RT_F * pH_grid, ls="--", lw=1.0, color="#333",
            alpha=0.7)

    ax.set_xlim(2, 10)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.40, 1.00)
    ax.set_xlabel("pH", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("E  /  V  vs  SHE", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=12, pad=8)
    ax.grid(True, ls=":", lw=0.4, alpha=0.4)

    # legend (only groups actually present)
    present = sorted(set(dom.flatten()))

# Re-run just the stack plots as PNG previews so I can inspect
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from speciation import solve_point, FE_T, CU_T, CIT_T
from make_plots import (FE_GROUPS, CU_GROUPS, FE_COLORS, CU_COLORS,
                        group_fraction, pH_grid, E_OXIC, E_REDUCE, E_MID,
                        cuts, citrate_partition)
import os

def stack_cut_png(records, groups, colors, total, kind, title, fname):
    names = [n for n, _ in groups]
    frac_arr = {n: np.zeros(len(records)) for n in names}
    for i, r in enumerate(records):
        if kind == "Fe":
            sp_dicts = [r["Fe3_species"], r["Fe2_species"]]
        else:
            sp_dicts = [r["Cu2_species"], r["Cu1_species"]]
        f = group_fraction(sp_dicts, groups, total, r["solids"], {})
        for n in names:
            frac_arr[n][i] = f[n]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4), dpi=110)
    stack = np.vstack([frac_arr[n] for n in names])
    ax.stackplot(pH_grid, stack, labels=names,
                 colors=[colors[n] for n in names],
                 edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.25)
    ax.set_xlim(2, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_xlabel("pH"); ax.set_ylabel(f"fraction of total {kind}")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11, pad=6)
    present = [n for n in names if frac_arr[n].max() > 0.01]
    handles = [Patch(facecolor=colors[n], edgecolor="#222", linewidth=0.4,
                     label=n) for n in present]
    ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper right",
              bbox_to_anchor=(1.38, 1.0), fontsize=8.5, frameon=False)
    ax.grid(True, ls=":", lw=0.4, alpha=0.4)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(f"figs/{fname}", bbox_inches="tight", dpi=110)
    plt.close(fig)

stack_cut_png(cuts[E_OXIC], FE_GROUPS, FE_COLORS, FE_T, "Fe",
              f"Fe speciation vs pH at E = {E_OXIC:+.2f} V (oxic)",
              "fe_vs_pH_oxic_preview.png")
stack_cut_png(cuts[E_OXIC], CU_GROUPS, CU_COLORS, CU_T, "Cu",
              f"Cu speciation vs pH at E = {E_OXIC:+.2f} V (oxic)",
              "cu_vs_pH_oxic_preview.png")
stack_cut_png(cuts[E_REDUCE], FE_GROUPS, FE_COLORS, FE_T, "Fe",
              f"Fe speciation vs pH at E = {E_REDUCE:+.2f} V (reducing)",
              "fe_vs_pH_reduce_preview.png")
stack_cut_png(cuts[E_REDUCE], CU_GROUPS, CU_COLORS, CU_T, "Cu",
              f"Cu speciation vs pH at E = {E_REDUCE:+.2f} V (reducing)",
              "cu_vs_pH_reduce_preview.png")

# citrate partition previews
for E_pick, tag in [(E_OXIC, "oxic"), (E_REDUCE, "reduce")]:
    free, by_Fe, by_Cu = citrate_partition(cuts[E_pick])
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.0), dpi=110)
    ax.stackplot(pH_grid, [by_Fe, by_Cu, free],
                 labels=["bound to Fe", "bound to Cu", "free / protonated"],
                 colors=["#7a3b17", "#2d4d7a", "#d0d0c4"],
                 edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)
    ax.set_xlim(2, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_xlabel("pH"); ax.set_ylabel("fraction of 5 mM citrate")
    ax.set_title(f"Citrate partitioning at E = {E_pick:+.2f} V ({tag})",
                 fontsize=11, pad=6)
    ax.legend(loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.32, 1.0), fontsize=9,
              frameon=False)
    ax.grid(True, ls=":", lw=0.4, alpha=0.4)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(f"figs/citrate_partition_{tag}_preview.png", bbox_inches="tight", dpi=110)
    plt.close(fig)

print("done previews")
EOF

**The setup.** 1 mM Fe(III), 1 mM Cu(II), 5 mM citrate, 0.1 M Cl⁻, 25 °C, I = 0.1 M, pH 2–10, E −0.4 to +1.0 V. The solver enforces the two mass balances plus Nernst on the Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ (E° = +0.771 V) and Cu²⁺/Cu⁺ (E° = +0.153 V) couples on a 81 × 71 grid; ferrihydrite, Cu(OH)₂(s), CuCl(s), and Cu(s) are tested for saturation and cap the free-ion activity when they form.

**How the competition actually plays out** (oxic, E = +0.60 V):

| pH | Fe verdict | Cu verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 2–3 | FeHCit⁺ (100 %) — log K = 12.3 with HCit²⁻ crushes FeCl_n | Cu²⁺ + CuCl⁺ (~99 %); citrate too protonated |
| 4–5 | FeHCit⁺ still (~99 %) | CuCit⁻ takes over (~88 %) |
| 6–7 | **Ferrihydrite** — Fe abandons citrate | CuCit⁻ / CuCit₂⁴⁻ (~50/50) |
| 8+ | ferrihydrite | **Cu(OH)₂(s)** — Cu drops out too |

The two metals **never actually fight over citrate**: 5 mM citrate is plenty for 2 mM total metal at 1:1, and the geometry of the Pourbaix diagram means that whenever one metal is bound to citrate, the other is either still there with room to spare (pH 4–5), already lost to a solid (Fe above pH 5.5), or freed by protonation (Cu below pH 4). Peak simultaneous citrate binding is at pH 5, where Fe holds ~20 % of the pool and Cu another ~20 %, leaving ~60 % free.

**Chloride's real job** is on the reduced side. It's a bit-player for Fe(III) (FeCl_n beaten by citrate by ~10 orders of magnitude) and marginal for Cu(II) (~20 % as CuCl⁺ at pH 2). But log β₂ = 5.5 for CuCl₂⁻ warps the Cu(II)/Cu(I) potential downward by ~330 mV, opening a large CuCl₂⁻ wedge between the Cu(s) line and the citrate belt (Figure 2 and Figure 4b).

**Every log K, log β, log \*K_s and E° the solver actually consumed** is in §2 of the report, with the primary source cited (Baes & Mesmer 1976 for hydrolysis, NIST 46 for chloride, Königsberger et al. 2000 and Silva et al. 2009 for Fe–citrate, Bard–Parsons–Jordan 1985 for potentials, Cornell & Schwertmann 2003 for ferrihydrite). §8 lists the biggest caveats — ferrihydrite solubility uncertainty, polynuclear Fe(III)–citrate species I omitted, and what happens if CO₂ is admitted — so you can see exactly which assumptions to relax if your system differs.
